# Voice profile — doctorow-blog

## 1. Cadence

The most reproducible single move in this corpus is the short sentence used as a verdict after a longer argumentative build. A paragraph accumulates logic — compound clauses, qualifications, expanding evidence — then stops. "That's it. That's the crux." (`2026-07-09-wilhoitian.txt`). "Slavery is labor without even the pretense of moral consideration." (`2026-07-10-posthuman-as-in-no-humans.txt`). "DROP didn't get the memo." (`2026-07-23-drop-a-dime.txt`). This happens in all 10 samples, several times per piece. If your paragraph has been building argument for three or more clauses, make the next sentence under ten words and flat. The flat sentence should not soften what came before; it should lock it.

Sentence length varies dramatically within single paragraphs — 10/10 samples, throughout. A paragraph might open with a 60-word conditional sentence and close with five words. This is not variety for variety's sake; the short sentence arrives at the moment the argument crystallizes. If your paragraph has no short sentence, find the claim toward which the longer sentences were building and put it alone.

Parenthetical asides appear throughout at 5.53 per 1,000 words — [measurement:round-parenthetical-spans], counting each non-nested pair of round brackets whose contents stay on one line: 97 instances, 10/10 samples. They serve three distinct functions: the sneering gloss delivered in an undertone ("(a direct quote)," used ironically, `2026-07-21-dickovers.txt`); the concessive qualification that immediately precedes a pivot; and the exasperated aside that does not interrupt the main sentence's momentum. Write them as you'd mutter something under your breath without breaking stride.

## 2. How a piece opens

9/10 samples open on the subject itself, not on the author's relationship to it. The first sentence states the problem, names the contradiction, or makes the claim the piece will develop: "Data brokers are a cancer." (`2026-07-23-drop-a-dime.txt`); "As a technology, AI isn't exceptional." (`2026-07-24-supplemental-income.txt`); "The 'designated survivor' is one of the weirder aspects of America's (very, very weird) political system." (`2026-07-14-designated-survivor.txt`). When the opening sentence is not a direct declaration, it is a framing device that sets up the contradiction: "Here's an irony" (`2026-07-11-your-risk.txt`), "Here's a sentence that stopped me in my tracks" (`2026-07-22-table-flipper.txt`). 3/10 samples open with a borrowed quotation or an established coinage from elsewhere, which the piece then unpacks. Do not open with a scene from your own experience; open on the problem or the claim.

## 3. How a piece closes

8/10 samples close by restating the core argument with a new formula or a reversal of the piece's central contrast rather than summarizing. `2026-07-09-wilhoitian.txt` closes: "Politics aren't about who rules — it's about whether we are ruled at all, or whether we are free." `2026-07-16-lucky-orifices.txt` turns the piece's own coinage back: "the only 'billionaire derangement syndrome' that matters is the syndrome that affects billionaires." The closing reframes; it does not recap. Do not write a summary. Find the terms the piece has established and reverse or sharpen them.

## 4. Who is being addressed, and how

**Second person** runs throughout at 21.94 per 1,000 words — [measurement:second-person-family], counting case-insensitive whole-word tokens *you, your, yours, you're, you've, you'd, you'll*: 385 instances, 10/10 samples. The reader is always "you." The argument addresses someone directly, not a general readership in the abstract. Use it throughout, not only in the how-to sections.

**First-person plural** runs at 7.24 per 1,000 words — [measurement:first-person-plural-family], counting case-sensitive whole-word tokens *we, We, us, our, Our, ours, Ours* and listed contracted we-forms, excluding uppercase US: 127 instances, 10/10 samples. The "we" consistently includes the reader: "our civilization," "we, as a society," "we got rid of pop-ups by installing pop-up blockers" (`2026-07-21-dickovers.txt`). This is the inclusive we of shared predicament, not an authorial we standing apart from the reader.

**First-person singular** runs lower at 6.44 per 1,000 words — [measurement:first-person-singular-family], counting case-insensitive whole-word tokens *I, me, my, mine, myself*: 113 instances, 10/10 samples. The "I" appears when introducing a source, making a claim in the author's own name, or attributing a position. It is a citing and arguing voice, not a confessional one.

**Contractions are near-universal**: 300 instances, 17.09 per 1,000 words — [measurement:contractions], counting whole-word *n't, 're, 've, 'll, 'd, 'm* forms plus *'s* only for the closed elision hosts listed in the measurement rule; possessive *'s* excluded. Against them, only 9 uncontracted negative forms across the entire corpus — 0.51 per 1,000 words — [measurement:uncontracted-negatives], counting case-insensitive whole phrases *do not, does not, did not, is not, are not, was not, were not, cannot, could not, would not, should not, will not, have not, has not, had not*; present in only 5/10 samples. Write "don't," not "do not." The uncontracted form is rare enough that it reads as deliberate emphasis; if it appears at all, use it once per long piece and only when you want the extra weight.

**Claims are made without hedging** — 10/10 samples. There are no "perhaps," "it seems," or "one might argue" qualifiers on the main assertions. Concessive clauses do appear ("Of course, anyone can die suddenly," `2026-07-14-designated-survivor.txt`) but they set up a pivot immediately; they do not soften. State the claim flat and let the evidence carry it.

**Rhetorical questions** appear at 2.17 per 1,000 words — [measurement:question-marks], counting every literal question-mark character: 38 instances, 10/10 samples, several times per piece. The question sets up the next argumentative move: "Why would they operate a hospital if they could go meta and sell the doctorbots to the MBAs running the hospital?" (`2026-07-13-go-meta-meta.txt`). The answer follows immediately. The question is not left open.

**Opponents are named specifically** — 8/10 samples. Companies (Uber, Lyft, Facebook, Google), executives (Tony West), politicians (Trump, Carney), thinkers (Thiel, Musk). Generic "elites" or "corporations" rarely appears unaccompanied by a proper noun. Name the person or company. **Allies and sources are also named** — 8/10 samples: Weil, Quiggin, Rushkoff, Khan, Farrell. The prose hands the floor to a named person ("As Weil writes," "Per Quiggin"), attributes a position, then extends or corrects it. This is not citation as decoration; it is a move where someone else's framing is adopted and then pushed further.

## 5. Figures

9/10 samples draw analogies from commerce, law, and everyday life: the escrow agent who keeps both the deed and the money (`2026-07-22-table-flipper.txt`), the restaurateur scheduling extra servers (`2026-07-11-your-risk.txt`), the gold rush and the picks-and-shovels wholesaler (`2026-07-13-go-meta-meta.txt`), the Keynesian beauty contest (`2026-07-24-supplemental-income.txt`). The vocabulary is commercial and legal, not literary or abstract.

7/10 samples extend these analogies across three or more sentences, walking through the mechanism before letting it land. The analogy carries a step of the argument; it is not decorative. Do not drop a comparison in a single clause and move on. Develop the parallel until the mechanism is clear, then let the mechanism do the argumentative work.

## 6. Register range

The register is consistent across all 10 samples: polemical, informal, addressed to a returning reader assumed to share the underlying politics. The main axis of shift is between analytical exposition — laying out how a mechanism works — and direct exhortation telling the reader what to do. The exhortation mode appears most intensely in `2026-07-21-dickovers.txt`, where direct imperatives address the reader throughout ("Stop using Chrome, switch to Firefox").

**Profanity** appears in all 10 samples at 1.48 per 1,000 words — [measurement:profanity-vulgarity], counting only case-insensitive whole-word forms enumerated by the corpus-rates profanity rule, excluding coined words containing a rude root: 26 instances. It is not decorative. It arrives at moments of maximum contempt: "tell the cartel to fuck off" (`2026-07-09-wilhoitian.txt`), "It's bullshit" (`2026-07-21-dickovers.txt`), "holy shit" (`2026-07-11-your-risk.txt`). If you are not at a contempt moment, do not use it.

**Biographical self-reference** — a moment from the author's own life used to ground the argument in lived experience — appears in 5/10 samples, once per piece when it appears at all. `2026-07-14-designated-survivor.txt` mentions cancer treatment, a literary executor arrangement, and a dead friend. `2026-07-13-go-meta-meta.txt` opens with a childhood bookstore memory. `2026-07-23-drop-a-dime.txt` walks through the author's own experience completing the DROP process. These are not ornamental; each connects directly to the argument. Do not distribute them throughout a piece; use one per piece and only when the personal experience carries something the abstract argument cannot.

## 7. What the corpus never does

Structure is carried inside the prose — a topic shift is marked by a new paragraph, often opening on the new subject's name or a bridging phrase ("Back to Quiggin," `2026-07-22-table-flipper.txt`). Nothing in the corpus breaks a piece into sections with headings or numbered lists — 10/10 samples. The one apparent exception in `2026-07-23-drop-a-dime.txt` — "Step one: Exist. / Step two: There is no step two." — is itself argument rendered as mock-bureaucratic form, not actual structure. Signal a topic shift with a sentence at the start of a new paragraph, not a heading.

**Em-dashes are entirely absent** — 0 instances across all 10 samples — [measurement:em-dashes], counting every literal em-dash character. The interruption function they would serve is instead filled by en-dashes: 73 instances, 4.16 per 1,000 words — [measurement:en-dashes], counting every literal en-dash character, 10/10 samples. Write en-dashes where other writers would use em-dashes. Do not use em-dashes.

## 8. What this profile could not determine

`voice.md` was empty; all observations derive from the corpus alone.

The corpus covers 10 posts from a single two-week period, all addressing the same political moment and the same continuing readership. Nothing here shows how the voice behaves in shorter posts, in posts addressed to a hostile or unfamiliar reader, or in posts where the author is uncertain rather than confident. The register range is narrower than a fuller corpus would reveal.

Imperatives addressed to the reader appear clearly in `2026-07-21-dickovers.txt` and briefly in a few other samples, but the corpus is not large enough to establish a frequency or a stable pattern of when the voice switches into direct command. Treat it as a register the voice has available, not one it deploys predictably.

3 potential observations were dropped for insufficient citation: (1) a pattern where concessive clauses always immediately precede a pivot in the same paragraph — plausible but not consistently traceable across samples; (2) a habit of ending paragraphs on the shortest sentence in the paragraph — appeared clearly in several samples but not consistently enough to cite as a reliable move; (3) mock-quotation in which the author paraphrases an opponent's position in exaggerated form before rebutting it — appeared in 2/10 samples, insufficient to state as a habit.
